In the counter affidavit, respondents 1 and 2 stated that there is no specific tenure fixed for a Managing Director of KINFRA and that as per Section 6 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Act, 1993 ('the Act' for short) which deals with the term of office of Managing Directors and conditions of services of nominated Director, the Managing Director of the Corporation shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify in this behalf.
The Directors shall be entitled to draw allowances as prescribed under the Rules made under the Act.

Under Rule 3 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Rules, 2008 the Directors nominated by the Government under sub section 2 of Section 5 shall ordinarily hold office for a term of 2 years.
However, the Government shall have the power to remove such Directors before the expiry of the said term, if found necessary.
The term of office of the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be as fixed by the Government in the order of appointment.
However, the Government may, at any time terminate the services of such Managing Director without assigning any reason.

Therefore, it is stated that it was upto the Government to fix the term and even if term is fixed, to order termination even before its expiry, as per the rules as well as Ext.R1(c) order issued by the Government on 20.05.2009.

It is stated that the litigation before the MadhyaPradesh High Court against M/s.Zoom Developers started during the tenure of petitioner and it resulted in adverse orders against KINFRA since petitioner did not take any steps to safeguard its interest.
9.
The additional respondent No.4 in his counter affidavit, explaining his qualifications, stated that he is fully qualified to be appointed as the Managing Director of KINFRA.

He was given additional charge of the KINFRA while terminating the appointment of the petitioner and that appointment was to a sector for which he had submitted application whereas there was no application from the petitioner for appointment in that sector.
He was initially appointed as the Managing Director of TRACO Cables Company under the Electrical Equipment category.

It is stated that he worked in senior management level as Director, Executive Director etc. during the last 20 years before his appointment as Managing Director.
10.
The petitioner filed reply affidavits to the counter affidavits of all the respondents.
He stated that even if no reason is to be assigned while terminating the services, reasons should be available in the files leading to the termination.

He stated that the notes furnished along with Ext.P20 letter dated 17.09.2019 of the State Public Information Officer do not reveal any reason for termination of his service; on the other hand it would appear that there was no reason at all as evident from the noting of the Principal Secretary that due process for removal was not followed as per the principles of natural justice.
According to the petitioner he was relieved at the instance of the Private Secretary to the Minister of Industries Department.

It was also pointed out that the information relating to the appearance of the concerned Government Pleader in the land acquisition cases who represented the state when his wife was the Counsel appearing for the claimants, was not brought to his notice by the official of KINFRA who was dealing with the matter; it is stated that he had already issued memos to that official for not furnishing the relevant information.
He also stated that the lease of land to M/s.Zoom Developers and its resumption in 2016 took place prior to his joining as the Managing Director.
It was also stated that he acted on the advice of the standing counsel of KINFRA.

Petitioner also produced Exts.P21 to P24 pointing out that his appointment as the Managing Director in KINFRA was on the basis of his performance in the interview whereas the application of the 4th respondent in the Development&Infrastructure sector was rejected and no other person was selected for KINFRA.

He also pointed out that Government have appointed Managing Directors in various Public Sector Undertakings from the select list prepared by the Public Enterprises Selection Board and the method of selection has been modified in 2019 and therefore the 4 th respondent is not a person who is selected in accordance with rules for appointment as the Managing Director of KINFRA.

11. Heard Sri. Vinod Madhavan, the learned Counsel for the petitioner, Mrs. M.R.Sreeletha, the learned Special Government Pleader for respondents 1 and 2 and Sri.Shylajan for the additional respondents 3 and 4.
12.

The main contention of the petitioner is that he was entitled to continue as the Managing Director for a period of three years, in the light of Ext.P7 order and that termination of his appointment before he completed his tenure is unsustainable.
But a perusal of the order of his appointment would show that no tenure is provided in it.

Under Section 6 of the KINFRA Act K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/
6 (Ext.R1(a))the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be appointed by the Government and he shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify.

sentences.text:
Even though the petitioner had requested to fix the terms and conditions of his appointment as per Ext.P6 and Ext.P6(a) letters on 07.10.2016 and 08.10.2016, it was only as per Ext.P8 order that the Government responded to that,
that too according sanction only for fixing his monthly remuneration at Rs.1.75 lakhs.

Nothing was stated regarding the term of appointment till Ext.P10 order was issued on 25.07.2019, fixing the term of his appointment upto 25.07.2019 and consequently terminating his appointment as Director from the Board of Directors, under section 6(2) of the Act.
Rule 4 deals with the appointment and term of office of Managing Director and conditions of service of the nominated directors.
Though the qualification, experience etc required for appointment are provided therein nothing is provided in the rules also regarding the term of the Managing Director.
Therefore, there is no basis for the contention that petitioner is entitled to continue as Managing Director either for a period of 3 years or for any particular period.
The contention that 3 months' notice is necessary for any termination as in the case of resignation, which is governed by Rule 8 is also baseless.
13. Ext.R1(c) Government order issued on 20.05.2009 provides for the pay structure as well as the general conditions of appointment of Chief Executive officers of the PSUs.
Clause 3 thereof provides that "appointment as MD/CEO of a Company/PSU shall be at the pleasure of the Government.
Government shall have the right to remove him from the post at any time (although the order of appointment will indicate a fixed term for such appointment).

If a person who holds the lien as employee in a company is appointed as CEO of a company and is later removed from the post of CEO he shall go back to the post where he holds such lien (unless he has crossed the age of superannuation in the parent company).
A person who does not have any lien in any company shall not have any right to continue in any of the PSUs.
Annexure to this Government order classifies the PSUs under various categories.
KINFRA - Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation is included in Annexure-II at serial no.5 of schedule A.
Therefore the petitioner was to hold office at the pleasure of Government.

As long as the provisions in the Act or Rules or even Ext.R1(c) order does not fix any fixed term for a Managing Director, the contention of the petitioner in the light of the tenure of the former Managing Directors that he is entitled to continue at least for a period of three years, is without any basis.

Even where a tenure is provided in the orders of appointment it is specifically stated in the Government order Ext.R1(c) that the Government shall have the right to remove the MD/CEO and his appointment shall be at the pleasure of the Government.

Therefore even if the order appointing the petitioner provided for a particular period like 3 years or more on his appointment, it was always open to the Government to terminate his appointment before expiry of the said period.
Therefore the orders Exts.P12 to P16 would not be of any help to the petitioner.

The fact that appointments were used to be made to the post of MD in the KINFRA for three years each or that further extensions were granted to those appointments would not be sufficient to hold that there is a minimum tenure for the appointment.
14. The next question is whether the Government should have stated any reason while terminating the appointment of the petitioner or at any rate the reasons should have been stated in the files.

When no term is fixed for the appointment, the question of reason in support of termination does K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/
7 not arise.

before the expiry of 5 years of his appointment, in contravention of section 12(7) of the KVASU Act,

Referring to the judgments of the apex court with respect to the doctrine of pleasure in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India: 2010 (6) SCC 331, this court held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily,
capriciously or whimsically.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was held therein that the discretionary powers conferred on public authority would be exercised reasonably and for public good.

It was found that the revocation of appointment of the Vice Chancellor was not for any administrative reason as it was found that the action was initiated on the basis of an article he had written and published in the Indian Express Newspaper.

The State Government was not able to explain the reason for recalling him from the post of Vice Chancellor and it was found that there was no bonafide administrative reason and in the absence of the same, recalling the appellant from the post of Vice Chancellor was an arbitrary and malafide action contrary to public interest and it was directed to restore him to the post of Vice Chancellor.
But in the present case no term was fixed and it cannot be said that there was a premature termination.

16. In the judgment in Union of India v. S.P.Sharma [(2014) 6 SCC 351], the Apex Court was considering a case where the termination of services of 2 Army personnel after court martial proceedings were defended in the light of Section 18 of the Army Act read with Article 310 of the Constitution, namely, exercise of doctrine of pleasure.

entities.text: Union of India v. S.P.Sharma [(2014) 6 SCC 351]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Army Personnel alleged violation of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution of India.

It was held that while exercising judicial review the court cannot substitute its own conclusions on the basis of materials on record, especially in a case where the safety and security of the nation was involved and the tenure of services of such army personnel are at the pleasure of the President and officers can be removed by the authority on whose pleasure he holds office without assigning any reason.
However it approved the constitution Bench judgment in B.P Singhal v. Union of India [(2010) 6 SCC 331].

entities.text: B.P Singhal v. Union of India [(2010) 6 SCC 331]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In B.P. Singhal's case he apex court while considering the question of removal of Governors held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily, capriciously or whimsically and that it is presumed that discretionary powers conferred on any public authority will necessarily be exercised reasonably and for the public good.

It was held that though no notice need be issued or reasons be assigned, there should be some valid cause for withdrawal of the pleasure and that it cannot be at the sweet will, whim and fancy of the authority.
It was also held that the controlling factor in determining whether the exercise of prerogative power is subject to judicial review is not its source but its subject-matter.
It was also held that the extent or scope of judicial review for one will be different from the scope of judicial review for the other.

It is pertinent to note that the order of appointment of petitioner did not K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/
8 contain any assurance to retain him for any particular period.

17. In the judgment in Retd. Armed Forces Medical Association & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors:
(2006) 11 SCC 731, relied on by the learned Government Pleader, the Apex Court was considering the validity of appointment of the Chief Engineer of the establishment as its Managing Director without fixing any tenure.

entities.text:
Retd. Armed Forces Medical Association & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors:
(2006) 11 SCC 731
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Apex Court held that when the Act and the Rules have not prescribed any definite term or any particular mode, the appointing authority has absolute discretion in the matter.
It was a case where a writ of quo-warranto was sought against the appellant therein.

The contention was that Section 6(1) of the Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Drainage Board Act 1973 which provided that the Managing Director shall hold office during the pleasure of the Government would not mean to have conferred any arbitrary or unfettered right to Government to retain him,
misusing its discretionary power to extend his tenure.

entities.text: Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Drainage Board Act 1973
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
In para.44 of the said judgment the Apex Court found as follows:
"44.
In the instant case, the power to appoint the Managing Director of the Board is vested in the Board under Section 4(2) of the Act.
Neither the Act nor the Rules prescribed any mode of appointment or tenure of appointment.

When the mode of appointment, tenure of appointment have been left to the discretion of the Government by the Act and the Rules, and the Act makes it clear that the Managing Director shall hold office at the pleasure of the Government, the High Court could not have fettered the discretion of the Government by holding that Section 4(2) of the Act does not expressly give the power to the State Government to make ad hoc or contractual appointment.

When the Act and the statutory Rules have not prescribed any definite term and any particular mode, the High Court could not have read into the statute a restriction or prohibition that is not expressly prohibited by the Act and the Rules.

It is well settled that when the statute does not lay down the method of appointment or term of appointment and when the Act specifies that the appointment is one of sure tenure, the appointing authority who has the power to appoint has absolute discretion in the matter and it cannot be said that discretion to appoint does not include the power to appoint on contract basis.
An appointment which is temporary remains temporary and does not become permanent with the passage of time.

The finding recorded by the learned Single Judge that the appointment is bad for the reason that the appointment which was made on temporary basis has continued for nearly 2 years is wholly contrary to law particularly when the Act and the Rules do not stipulate maximum period of appointment.
The High Court, in our view, gravely erred in issuing a writ of quo warranto when there is no clear violation of law in the appointment of the appellant."
It was held that there was no disqualification for the Managing Director to continue and that the court cannot sit in judgment over the wisdom of the Government.
It was a case where appointment was challenged whereas in this case the termination is under challenge.

18. It is relevant to note the judgment in WP(C) No.29558/2017, relied on by the learned Government Pleader where the petitioner sought re-appointment as a Managing Director stating K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/
9 that he was only relieved from the post and there was no termination.

sentences.text: He was initially appointed as Managing Director of Quilon Cooperative Spinning Mills on 25.06.2013; on 21.05.2014 he was appointed as the Managing Director of another Public Sector Undertaking; on 03.06.2015 he was appointed as the Managing Director of yet another Public Sector Undertaking; on 15.10.2015 he was appointed as the Executive Director of yet another Public Sector Undertaking; he was relieved on 18.06.2016 while giving additional charge to another person.
He claimed further appointments pointing out that he was only relieved.
Government stated that vigilance cases were going on and it was not prudent to entrust him to run any organization.
He pointed out that there was no allegation against him in the FIR.

The writ petition was dismissed as there is no provision of law which provides that once a person is appointed as Managing Director he is liable to be retained as Managing Director of one or other Public Sector Undertakings or that he can continue for a particular tenure.

19. In this case respondents have produced Ext.R1(i) directing Vigilance enquiry into the loss caused to KINFRA on account of lapses in conducting the case before Madhyapradesh High Court for failure to take steps to protect its interest of KINFRA.
Therefore the decision of the respondents to terminate the appointment does not require any interference.

In the absence of any rules prescribing any fixed term for the Managing Director of KINFRA, it cannot be said that petitioner is entitled to continue for any fixed period or that the termination can be effected only after issuing notice.

20. However the case of the petitioner that the respondents want to save the real culprits behind the issue which arose in respect of the land acquisition at Ramanattukara, as the termination is effected immediately after he issued show cause notice to the official who was dealing with those matters and his contention about the intention of the respondents to save M/s.Zoom Developers and to save the real culprits behind all these, deserves serious consideration.

Though the respondents have stated that vigilance proceedings are initiated as per Government letter No.Vig-B1/335/19-Vig dated 25.10.2019, no steps are seen taken to expedite the same and to book the real culprits.
Therefore the respondents shall see that the Vigilance enquiry in these matters are expedited and appropriate action is taken in accordance with law.
The writ petition is dismissed with the above observation.

opennyai_summary.facts:
Petitioner was appointed as Managing Director of KINFRA, as per Ext.P4 order, under section 6 of Chapter III of Act 3 of 1993-the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation Act.
It was ordered that his continuance in the post would be subject to the clearance from the Director of Vigilance and Anti Corruption Bureau and that the terms and conditions of the appointment would be fixed later.
opennyai_summary.arguments:
Under Rule 3 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Rules, 2008 the Directors nominated by the Government under sub section 2 of Section 5 shall ordinarily hold office for a term of 2 years.
The main contention of the petitioner is that he was entitled to continue as the Managing Director for a period of three years, in the light of Ext.P7 order and that termination of his appointment before he completed his tenure is unsustainable.
But a perusal of the order of his appointment would show that no tenure is provided in it.
Even though the petitioner had requested to fix the terms and conditions of his appointment as per Ext.P6 and Ext.P6(a) letters on 07.10.2016 and 08.10.2016, it was only as per Ext.P8 order that the Government responded to that,
that too according sanction only for fixing his monthly remuneration at Rs.1.75 lakhs.
15. The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the judgment of the Division Bench in Ashok v.
Chancellor, Kerala Veterinary and Animal Sciences University : 2012 (3) KLT 829 and the judgment of the Apex Court in Union of India and others vs. Major S.P.Sharma and others : (2014) 6 SCC 351 in support of his contention that the termination was illegal, in the absence of availability of any reasons at least in the files, even when the petitioner held his appointment at the pleasure of Government.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Under Section 6 of the KINFRA Act K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/
6 (Ext.R1(a))the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be appointed by the Government and he shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify.
Nothing was stated regarding the term of appointment till Ext.P10 order was issued on 25.07.2019, fixing the term of his appointment upto 25.07.2019 and consequently terminating his appointment as Director from the Board of Directors, under section 6(2) of the Act.
Though the qualification, experience etc required for appointment are provided therein nothing is provided in the rules also regarding the term of the Managing Director.
Therefore, there is no basis for the contention that petitioner is entitled to continue as Managing Director either for a period of 3 years or for any particular period.
Therefore the petitioner was to hold office at the pleasure of Government.
As long as the provisions in the Act or Rules or even Ext.R1(c) order does not fix any fixed term for a Managing Director, the contention of the petitioner in the light of the tenure of the former Managing Directors that he is entitled to continue at least for a period of three years, is without any basis.
Even where a tenure is provided in the orders of appointment it is specifically stated in the Government order Ext.R1(c) that the Government shall have the right to remove the MD/CEO and his appointment shall be at the pleasure of the Government.
Therefore even if the order appointing the petitioner provided for a particular period like 3 years or more on his appointment, it was always open to the Government to terminate his appointment before expiry of the said period.
Therefore the orders Exts.P12 to P16 would not be of any help to the petitioner.
The fact that appointments were used to be made to the post of MD in the KINFRA for three years each or that further extensions were granted to those appointments would not be sufficient to hold that there is a minimum tenure for the appointment.
But in the present case no term was fixed and it cannot be said that there was a premature termination.
However it approved the constitution Bench judgment in B.P Singhal v. Union of India [(2010) 6 SCC 331].
17. In the judgment in Retd. Armed Forces Medical Association & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors:
(2006) 11 SCC 731, relied on by the learned Government Pleader, the Apex Court was considering the validity of appointment of the Chief Engineer of the establishment as its Managing Director without fixing any tenure.
The writ petition was dismissed as there is no provision of law which provides that once a person is appointed as Managing Director he is liable to be retained as Managing Director of one or other Public Sector Undertakings or that he can continue for a particular tenure.
19. In this case respondents have produced Ext.R1(i) directing Vigilance enquiry into the loss caused to KINFRA on account of lapses in conducting the case before Madhyapradesh High Court for failure to take steps to protect its interest of KINFRA.
Therefore the decision of the respondents to terminate the appointment does not require any interference.
In the absence of any rules prescribing any fixed term for the Managing Director of KINFRA, it cannot be said that petitioner is entitled to continue for any fixed period or that the termination can be effected only after issuing notice.
opennyai_summary.issue: 14. The next question is whether the Government should have stated any reason while terminating the appointment of the petitioner or at any rate the reasons should have been stated in the files.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Though the respondents have stated that vigilance proceedings are initiated as per Government letter No.Vig-B1/335/19-Vig dated 25.10.2019, no steps are seen taken to expedite the same and to book the real culprits.
Therefore the respondents shall see that the Vigilance enquiry in these matters are expedited and appropriate action is taken in accordance with law.
The writ petition is dismissed with the above observation.
